title: Hagar names God (Genesis 16)
hookLine: a runaway servant meets an angel at a spring and calls God "the God who sees me"

cards: Ten years in the land, and still no child. So Sarai does something that is hard to hear today. She gives her Egyptian servant, Hagar, to Abram, hoping for a child through her.
Hagar conceives, and the household cracks. Hagar looks down on Sarai. Sarai treats her harshly.
And Hagar, pregnant and alone, runs away into the desert, on the road to Shur. She stops at a spring of water in the wilderness, and there, the Torah says, an angel of the LORD finds her.
In a big, rich household, she is the foreign servant, the one nobody asks. And she is the one the angel comes looking for.

teach.b: The angel speaks first, and the first word is her name. In the old JPS translation: "Hagar, Sarai's handmaid, whence camest thou? and whither goest thou?"
Notice this: in the whole chapter, Sarai and Abram never once say her name. They call her my handmaid, thy maid. The angel is the first to call her Hagar.
Then the hard part. The angel tells her to go back to her mistress.
Readers have struggled with that, and some commentators, like Nachmanides, said openly that Sarai did wrong in afflicting her, and Abram did wrong in allowing it.
But the angel also gives her a promise of her own: a son, and many descendants.
Call him Ishmael, the angel says, which means God hears, because God has heard your affliction. Then Hagar does something remarkable. She gives God a name of her own: El Roi.

teach.h: EL ROI — GOD WHO SEES ME.
teach.b: "Thou art a God of seeing," in the JPS wording: the God who sees me. The spring gets a name too: Beer-lahai-roi, the well of the Living One who sees me. A servant nobody named is named by an angel.

teach.h: THOU ART A GOD OF SEEING.
teach.b: A woman nobody listened to is told that God heard her. And the one nobody saw names God as the one who sees. Her son's name means God hears; her name for God means God sees.
In one chapter, a servant with no power at all is given both.

how: Jews read Hagar's story in the Torah portion Lech Lecha, and her name for God, El Roi, the God who sees me, is often taught as a reminder to notice people who are overlooked.

o: the God who truly sees me
the God of the desert well

p: the well of the Living One who sees me

the commentators all defend how Sarai treated Hagar

games.q: you're Hagar, alone at a spring in the desert. an angel has just called you by name and promised you a son. what do you do?
o: give God a name: the God who sees me.
ask the angel to take you home.
games.why: she names God El Roi, the God who sees me. the spring is named for it too: Beer-lahai-roi.

practice: Picture one person you pass every day without really seeing: the person who cleans the office, the cashier, the bus driver, the quiet kid in the group chat, the neighbor you only know by their dog.
See their face as clearly as you can, and ask yourself whether you know their name. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer; if not, just see them, fully, for a minute.

wordCard.voice: El Roi. The God who sees me: Hagar's name for God. That's the sixth week: Babel, lech lecha, midrash, Egypt, Lot's choice, the stars, and El Roi.

orig.note: Hebrew: God of seeing, the God who sees me. Hagar's name for God.

carryVoice: Your line: you are seen. Hagar was, at a spring in the desert. Six weeks, done.
